t: Flip Game II — Minimax, Memoization, and Sprague–Grundy
o:
## Understanding the problem

Two players alternately replace any occurrence of the substring `"++"` with `"--"`. Whoever cannot move loses, so we must decide whether the **first** player has a winning strategy.

**Example 1:** `"++++"` → `true`. If player 1 flips the middle pair to get `"+--+"`, the board has no `"++"`, so player 2 is stuck immediately. (Flipping an end pair, e.g. `"--++"`, would lose, since player 2 flips the remaining pair.)

**Example 2:** `"+"` → `false`. A lone `+` offers no legal move, so the first player loses instantly.

The constraints hint at what is feasible: length up to 60, but **no more than 20 consecutive `+`**. A naive game tree is astronomically large, yet the number of *distinct* positions reachable from one run of $k$ pluses equals the number of matchings of a path graph, which is only $F_{k+1}$ (Fibonacci) — at most $F_{21} \approx 10^4$ for $k=20$. This makes memoized search viable, and also enables a closed-form game-theory solution.
k: A position is winning iff some move leads to a losing position for the opponent — classic minimax on the string state.
Only runs of consecutive '+' matter; '-' cells never participate in moves, so the game splits into independent subgames.
Reachable states from a run of k pluses grow like Fibonacci F(k+1), so memoization collapses the exponential game tree.
By the Sprague–Grundy theorem, the answer is the XOR of Grundy values g[len] of each maximal '+' run, where g[n] = mex{ g[i] ^ g[n-2-i] }.

a.i: Try every possible flip. After making a flip, recursively ask whether the opponent can win from the resulting position. If **any** move makes the opponent lose, the current position is winning. This directly encodes the minimax definition of an impartial normal-play game and needs no extra data structures — just undo the move after recursing.
s: Scan the string left to right for each occurrence of "++".
Flip that pair to "--", recursively evaluate whether the opponent wins from the new state.
If any recursion returns false (opponent cannot force a win), return true.
If no move yields a win, return false; a string with no "++" returns false immediately.
a.t: Exponential — the recurrence T(n) = sum over moves of T(n-2) behaves like a double factorial, roughly O(n!!) in the worst case (e.g. a long run of pluses).
a.sp: O(n) recursion depth; the board itself is modified in place.

a.i: The same string position is reached through many different move orders, so cache the win/lose verdict per string. Since a run of $k$ pluses admits only $F_{k+1}$ distinct descendant configurations (matchings of a path), and runs are capped at 20, the memo stays tiny ($\le F_{21} \approx 11{,}000$ entries per run). Each evaluation tries at most $O(L)$ moves costing $O(L)$ string work, so the search becomes polynomial-in-practice despite the exponential game tree.
s: Maintain a hash map from string to its computed win/lose value.
On entry, return the cached verdict if present.
For each "++" occurrence, build the successor string with that pair flipped.
If the successor is a loss for the mover's opponent, record and return true.
Otherwise record false and return it.
a.t: O(S * L) where S is the number of distinct reachable states (at most the product of Fibonacci numbers F(run_len + 1), dominated by F(21) since runs are capped at 20) and L <= 60 is the string length used for hashing/copying.
a.sp: O(S * L) for the memo plus O(L) recursion depth.

a.i: A flip inside a run of $k$ consecutive pluses splits it into two independent runs of lengths $i$ and $k-2-i$. Independent impartial games combine by XOR of their Grundy values, so define $g[n] = \mathrm{mex}\{\, g[i] \oplus g[n-2-i] : 0 \le i \le n-2 \,\}$ with $g[0]=g[1]=0$. The whole position is losing exactly when the XOR of $g[\text{run}]$ over all maximal `+` runs is zero. This reduces the problem to a one-time $O(G^2)$ table computation ($G=60$) and an $O(n)$ scan — no search at all.
s: Precompute g[0..60]: g[0] = g[1] = 0; for larger n take the mex of g[i] XOR g[n-2-i] over all valid splits.
Split currentState into maximal runs of consecutive '+' characters.
XOR the Grundy value of each run length into an accumulator.
Return true iff the accumulator is nonzero.
a.t: O(G^2 + n) with G = 60 — building the Grundy table dominates once; each query is a linear scan.

w:
## Wrap-up

In an interview, lead with **brute-force minimax** (it shows you understand game trees), then upgrade to **memoization** when asked about efficiency — this is the expected solution and the natural place to derive the runtime: reachable states from a run of $k$ pluses follow the Fibonacci-style count $F_{k+1}$, so with runs capped at 20 the memo holds at most ~$F_{21}$ strings, each processed in $O(L)$, i.e. effectively $O(L \cdot \varphi^{L})$ worst case but trivially fast here. Mention **Sprague–Grundy** as the elegant $O(n)$ finisher if the interviewer pushes for optimality or asks the follow-up explicitly.

Common pitfalls: forgetting to restore the board after the recursive call; using `i < n` instead of `i + 1 < n` (out-of-bounds reads); in the Grundy version, treating runs of length 0 or 1 incorrectly (both have $g=0$, contributing nothing to the XOR — handle them implicitly rather than specially).

Likely follow-ups: derive the exact runtime of the memoized search (Fibonacci-bounded state space); solve Flip Game I (enumerate all reachable next states); generalize to flipping $m$ consecutive pluses (same framework, adjust the recurrence); or prove why XOR-of-Grundy-values characterizes N-positions in sums of impartial games.
